title: 14 — Design a Video Platform (YouTube)
html:
14 — Design a Video Platform (YouTube)

The one idea: videos never pass through your API servers. Clients upload directly to blob storage with a pre-signed URL; a transcoding DAG turns the original into many resolutions and formats; viewers stream adaptive-bitrate segments from a CDN. Cost is dominated by CDN egress, so the design question is what to put on the CDN.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Upload and watch videos; mobile, web, smart TV.
  • 5M DAU, 30 min/day watch time; international users.
  • Most resolutions and formats; encryption; max video size 1 GB.
  • Use existing cloud infrastructure (blob storage, CDN).

Estimates

  • 10% of users upload 1 video/day; avg 300 MB → 5M × 10% × 300 MB = 150 TB/day of new storage.
  • CDN cost: at ~$0.02/GB and 5 videos watched/user/day → 5M × 5 × 0.3 GB × $0.02 ≈ $150,000/day. → CDN strategy is the design driver.

Step 2 — High-level design

---
title: Video platform — upload and streaming architecture
---
flowchart LR
    Client["Client"] -->|"stream"| CDN["CDN"]
    Client -->|"everything else"| API["API servers"]
    API --> MDB[("Metadata DB + cache")]
    Client -->|"upload (pre-signed URL)"| OS[("Original storage")]
    OS --> TS["Transcoding servers"]
    TS --> TStore[("Transcoded storage")]
    TStore --> CDN
    TS --> CQ["Completion queue"] --> CH["Completion handler"] --> MDB

Upload flow

  1. Client requests an upload → API returns a pre-signed URL for object storage.
  2. Client uploads directly (in parallel, resumable chunks).
  3. Storage event triggers transcoding.
  4. In parallel, the client sends metadata (title, description) to the API.
  5. Transcoding completes → event on a completion queue → handler updates metadata (status, URLs).

Streaming

  • Protocols: HLS, MPEG-DASH — video split into small segments (2–10 s) at multiple bitrates, described by a manifest.
  • Adaptive bitrate (ABR): the player switches bitrate per segment based on bandwidth.
  • Streams come from the nearest CDN edge.

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Transcoding

Why: raw video is huge; devices support different codecs/containers; ABR needs multiple renditions.

  • Container: .mp4, .webm, .mov
  • Codec: H.264, VP9, HEVC, AV1

3.2 The DAG model

Different creators need different processing (watermarks, thumbnails, HD). Model transcoding as a directed acyclic graph of tasks:

---
title: Video transcoding DAG
---
flowchart LR
    O["Original"] --> SV["Split: video"]
    O --> SA["Split: audio"]
    O --> SM["Metadata"]
    SV --> I["Inspect"]
    SV --> E1["Encode 360p"]
    SV --> E2["Encode 720p"]
    SV --> E3["Encode 1080p"]
    SV --> T["Thumbnails"]
    SV --> W["Watermark"]
    SA --> AE["Audio encode"]
    E1 --> M["Assemble + manifest"]
    E2 --> M
    E3 --> M
    AE --> M

Architecture: preprocessor (splits into GOP-aligned chunks, builds the DAG from config, caches segments) → DAG scheduler (stages tasks into a queue) → resource manager (task queue, worker queue, running queue; picks optimal worker) → task workers → encoded video.

3.3 Speed

  • Parallel upload of GOP-aligned chunks; resumable on failure.
  • Upload centres close to users (regional storage endpoints).
  • Parallelism everywhere: message queues between stages so each scales independently.

3.4 Safety

  • Pre-signed URLs — only authorised uploads, time-limited.
  • DRM (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady), AES encryption of segments, watermarking.

3.5 Cost optimisation

Popularity follows a long tail:

  • Serve only popular videos from the CDN; the long tail from origin/cheaper servers.
  • Encode unpopular videos on demand or with fewer renditions; short videos with fewer formats.
  • Regional popularity → don't distribute everywhere.
  • Build your own CDN / ISP partnerships at very large scale (Netflix Open Connect).

3.6 Error handling

Error Handling
Upload fails Retry the chunk
Split fails Server-side split if the client is old
Transcoding fails Retry the task
Preprocessor/DAG scheduler down Reschedule pending tasks
Worker down Retry on another worker
API server down Stateless → next server
Metadata cache/DB down Replicas; promote a replica

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Scale the API tier (stateless), scale the DB (replication + sharding), live streaming (lower latency, less parallelism, different protocols like WebRTC/LL-HLS), and takedowns (copyright, policy).

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Upload: Blob Storage with a SAS token (user-delegation SAS via BlobClient.GenerateUserDelegationSasUri); client uses block blobs (StageBlock + CommitBlockList) for parallel, resumable uploads.
  • Trigger: Event Grid BlobCreated → Service Bus → transcoding workers.
  • Transcoding: FFmpeg in Container Apps jobs / AKS with GPU node pools (Azure Media Services has been retired — plan for self-managed FFmpeg or a partner service).
  • Workflow/DAG: Durable Functions fan-out/fan-in is a natural fit for the per-rendition tasks.
  • Delivery: Front Door / Azure CDN in front of the transcoded container; hot/cool/archive tiers for the long tail.
  • Metadata: Azure SQL or Cosmos DB; view counts via Redis counters flushed periodically.

Review checklist

  • CDN cost estimate → drives the design.
  • Direct-to-storage upload with pre-signed URLs.
  • Transcoding as a DAG; parallel chunks.
  • ABR streaming (HLS/DASH) from CDN.
  • Long-tail cost optimisation.
  • Error handling per component.
